boy.qwen_voice: A 7-year-old boy with a bright, clear, warm child's voice, curious and natural, light humor, never shouting, like a friendly kid host.

uncle.qwen_voice: A big, warm, middle-aged man with a deep, rich, jolly voice, a little husky, funny and affectionate, able to turn quiet and sincere.

grandma.qwen_voice: An elderly woman, a kind village cook, with a warm, slightly raspy voice, brisk and teasing, patient with children.

narrator.qwen_voice: A deep, calm, solemn male storyteller voice with a slow measured pace, like the narrator of an ancient legend.

lines.text: Hot soup, inside a dumpling... in a skin you can almost see through. How?
lines.qwen: Delivery: hushed, amazed, half to himself.

lines.text: Welcome to The Dumpling Boy! Stick around, and my uncle will show you what not to do.
lines.qwen: Delivery: warm, amused, to the lens.

lines.text: I'm fine.
lines.qwen: Delivery: muffled by an ice pack, dignified.

lines.text: The Silk Road? Never one road, you know. Loads of them, by land and sea.
lines.qwen: Delivery: easy, storyteller, a little smile.

lines.text: Near Shanghai there was a port, Qinglong. Over a thousand years ago, its ships carried pottery to Japan and Korea.
lines.qwen: Delivery: leaning in, interested, then wondering on the last half.

lines.text: Dad's first page just says: Shanghai. Be patient. The soup is the secret.
lines.qwen: Delivery: softly, reading, thinking it over.

lines.text: Mm... dumplings...
lines.qwen: Delivery: slurred, dreamy, talking in his sleep.

lines.text: This is Nanxiang, an old canal town. These days, it's part of Shanghai.
lines.qwen: Delivery: relaxed, glad to be here.

lines.text: Two little brick pagodas, about a thousand years old.
A thousand?
The temple burned in 1766. They're still standing.
Things that last. I like that.
lines.qwen: Delivery: soft, a little moved, then a held beat.

lines.text: Hello! Um, how do you get soup inside?
lines.qwen: Delivery: bright, curious, a little shy.

lines.text: Everyone asks. You don't pour it in. You make it a jelly first.
lines.qwen: Delivery: brisk, teasing, eyes on her hands.

lines.text: Pork skin, boiled for hours. Cold, it sets. Then I chop it, fold it into the meat.
Huh.
Then the steam melts it back into soup. That's why you never boil them.
lines.qwen: Delivery: low, dreamy, a cook who knows.

lines.text: Wait, really? The soup goes in solid?
How many folds?
Fourteen, sixteen, eighteen. Every cook has a number. Mine's eighteen.
...six, seven... oh, hang on.
Start again, dear.
Slowly, slowly!
Uncle, wait. There's soup inside!
Relax. For dumpling research!
lines.qwen: Delivery: grand, relaxed, waving him off.

lines.text: ...There was soup inside.
Mm-hm. Everyone learns once.
Breathe, Uncle.
Okay, watch. Lift it by the top knot, like this. Then onto a spoon.
A tiny hole, to let the steam out.
Then we wait?
Good. Soup first.
Better?
Oh... that's good. For dumpling research.
Now the dumpling, with a little black vinegar and ginger.
So who made the very first one?
Legend says: around the year 1871, a shop in Nanxiang sold one very big meat bun.
He made it smaller. And inside, he hid soup, set as jelly.
It became famous by getting smaller.
That's not what he looked like.
He had my energy.
lines.qwen: Delivery: dignified, not lowering the spoon.

lines.text: Many towns claim this dumpling. So: legend says.
That hat... A man sat on that stool, years ago. He burned his tongue, too.
lines.qwen: Delivery: slowing down, then quiet and a little amazed.

lines.text: My... dad?
Dad wrote... rush it, you get burned. Be patient, you get the best part.
lines.qwen: Delivery: quiet, reading aloud, his voice a little tight.

lines.text: Your dad picked a good first page.
...Yeah.
lines.qwen: Delivery: a small smile, almost a breath.

lines.text: Then he went south. To Guangzhou.
More dumplings?
Dad was right... the best part is worth the wait.
lines.qwen: Delivery: soft, to the lens, a small smile.
